name: NeoGraft

lead: NeoGraft is a machine that automates part of FUE hair transplant harvesting, used to fill thinning areas for fuller coverage. Wikipedia describes it as the first robotic surgical device FDA-approved for hair restoration, in 2009.

Grokipedia describes it as using pneumatic pressure to extract and deliver grafts without twisting or pulling. Little outcome data has been published, and no comparison with other harvesting methods was identified.

paras: Follicular units are extracted from the donor scalp by pneumatic suction-assisted extraction, then implanted in thinning areas as in FUE.
Risks match FUE generally. A surgeon abstract presented in 2014 argued that most hair-restoration patients are not appropriate FUE candidates, whether extraction is manual or with NeoGraft or ARTAS.

angle.text: NeoGraft is an automated suction-assisted FUE device, reported FDA-approved in 2009, used to harvest and deliver grafts for hair transplants that restore coverage. Little outcome data has been published.

lead: NeoGraft is an automated device used for follicular unit extraction (FUE), a hair transplant method in which individual hair follicles are harvested from the back and sides of the scalp and relocated to thinning or bald areas. People use it to restore hairline and density without the linear scar of a strip harvest. [1]

Wikipedia describes it as the first robotic surgical device FDA-approved for hair restoration, in 2009, and notes that FUE leaves small punctate donor scars and shorter recovery than strip surgery. [1] A review of suction-assisted extraction traces it to the Punch Hair Matic SAFER launched by Medicamat in 2005, sold in the US as NeoGraft, with a redesigned version launched in 2012. [2] Venus Concept is its exclusive US distributor. [3]

The device uses a rotating punch with suction that carries each graft into a saline-filled canister, replacing the forceps-removal step. [2][4] Proponents say this can speed up extraction and reduce handling trauma; the review notes such advantages have not all been consistently realised. [2] A surgeon abstract presented in 2014 argued that most hair-restoration patients are not appropriate FUE candidates, whether extraction is manual or with NeoGraft or the ARTAS robot.  No published trial comparing NeoGraft with other harvesting methods was identified.
infobox: Cleared as a Class I device for suction-assisted follicular extraction and re-implantation (per distributor) [3]

paras: Standard FUE has two steps: punching around the graft and removing it with forceps. Suction-assisted extraction replaces the forceps step with suction that carries each graft into a collection canister. The NeoGraft handpiece uses a rotating punch of 0.8 to 1.25 mm external diameter, with about 2 to 3 psi of suction; grafts are held in saline in a canister of about 300 to 350 grafts. [2]

The manufacturer's distributor says an automated handpiece extracts follicles, which are then separated and implanted; sessions run roughly 4 to 10 hours under local anesthesia, and shedding of transplanted hairs around days 3 to 4 is described as normal. [3]

Claimed advantages of suction-assisted FUE include a faster procedure, fewer assistants, less trauma during removal and a cleaner field. A review says it possibly reduces transection risk but that not all benefits are consistently realised. [2] Early concerns about graft drying from vacuum airflow are described as diminished with fluid-filled canisters. [2]

Wikipedia describes risks of hair transplantation generally, including temporary shock loss, infection and reduced graft survival from smoking, and notes FUE is physically demanding for surgeons with a steep learning curve. [1]

The 2014 meeting abstract states that hairs survive in a new location only as long as they would have in the donor area, and that FUE candidacy is limited by donor supply. [4] Wikipedia notes patients may be screened with the debated fox test and that body hair transplantation is possible only with FUE. [1]
